Encoding High-level Quantum Programs as SZX-diagrams
Augustin Borgna, Rafael Romero

Abstract
The Scalable ZX-calculus is a compact graphical language used to reason about linear maps between quantum states. These diagrams have multiple applications, but they frequently have to be constructed in a case-by-case basis. In this work we present a method to encode quantum programs implemented in a fragment of the linear dependently typed Proto-Quipper-D language as families of SZX-diagrams. We define a subset of translatable Proto-Quipper-D programs and show that our procedure is able to encode non-trivial algorithms as diagrams that grow linearly on the size of the program.



1
Introduction

The ZX calculus
[
19
]
has been used as intermediary representation language
for quantum programs in optimization methods
[
13
,
6
,
4
]

and in the design of error correcting schemes
[
5
]
.
The highly flexible representation of linear maps as open graphs
with a complete formal rewriting system
and the multiple extensions adapted to represent
different sets of quantum primitives
have proven useful in reasoning about the properties of quantum circuits.

Quantum operations are usually represented as quantum circuits
composed by primitive gates operating over a fixed number of qubits.
The ZX calculus has a close correspondence to this model and is similarly
limited to representing operations at a single-qubit level.
In this work we will focus on the Scalable ZX extension
[
8
]
,
which generalizes the ZX diagrams to work with arbitrary qubit registers
using a compact representation.
Previous work
[
7
]
has shown that the SZX calculus
is capable of encoding nontrivial algorithms
via the presentation of multiple hand-written examples.
For an efficient usage as an intermediate representation language,
we require an automated compilation method from quantum programming languages to SZX diagrams.
While ZX diagrams can be directly obtained from a program compiled to a quantum circuit,
to the best of our knowledge there is no efficient method leveraging the parametricity of the SZX calculus.

There exist several quantum programming languages capable of encoding
high-level parametric programs
[
2
,
12
,
18
]
.
Quipper
[
16
]
is a language for quantum computing
capable or generating families of quantum operations indexed by parameters.
These parameters need to be instantiated at compile time to generate
concrete quantum circuit representations.
Quipper has multiple formal specifications, in this work we focus on the
linear dependently typed Proto-Quipper-D formalization
[
15
,
14
]

to express high-level programs with integer parameters.

The contributions of this article the following.
We introduce a
list initialization
notation to represent multiple elements
of a SZX diagram family composed in parallel.
We formally define a fragment of Proto-Quipper-D programs that can be described as families of diagrams.
Then we present a novel compilation method that encodes quantum programs as families of SZX diagrams
and demonstrate the codification and translation of a nontrivial algorithm using our procedure.

In Section
2
we outline both languages and introduce the list
initialization notation. In Section
3
we define the restricted
Proto-Quipper-D fragment. In Section
4
we introduce the
translation into SZX diagrams. Finally, in Section
5
we
demonstrate an encoding of the Quantum Fourier Transform algorithm using our
method. The proofs of the lemmas stated in this work can be found
in
Appendix
E
.

2
Background

We describe a quantum state as a system of
n
qubits
corresponding to a vector in the
\mathbb{C}^{2^{n}}
Hilbert space.
We may partition the set of qubits into multi-qubit
registers

representing logically related subsets.
Quantum computations under the QRAM model correspond to compositions of unitary
operators between these quantum states, called quantum gates.
Additionally, the qubits may be initialized on a set state and measured.

High-level programs can be encoded in Quipper
[
16
]
,
a Haskell-like programming language for describing quantum computations.
In this work we use a formalization of the language called
Proto-Quipper-D
[
14
]
with support for linear and dependent types.
Concrete quantum operations correspond to linear functions between quantum states,
generated as a composition of primitive operations that can be described directly
as a quantum circuit.
Generic circuits may have additional parameters that must fixed at compilation time
to produce the corresponding quantum circuit.

In Section
3
we describe a restricted fragment of the Proto-Quipper-D
language containing the relevant operations for the work presented in this paper.

[

is a formal graphical language
that encodes linear maps between quantum states.

where
n_{k}
represents the n-tensor of k-qubit registers,
the green and red nodes are called Z and X spiders,

\alpha\in[0,2\pi)
is the phase of the spiders,
and the yellow square is called the Hadamard node.
These primitives allow us to encode any quantum operation,
but they can become impractical when working with multiple qubit registers.

The SZX calculus
[
8
,
7
]

is a
Scalable
extension to the ZX-calculus
that generalizes the primitives to work with arbitrarily sized qubit registers.
This facilitates the representation of diagrams with repeated structure
in a compact manner.
Carette et al.
[
7
]
show that the scalable and grounded extensions
can be directly composed.
Will refer to the resulting
\text{SZX}_{\hbox to7.4pt{\vbox to4.21pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 3.7pt\lower-2.50708pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}

-calculus as SZX for simplicity.
Bold wires in a SZX diagram are tagged with a non-negative integer representing
the size of the qubit register they carry, and other generators are marked in bold
to represent a parallel application over each qubit in the register.
Bold spiders with multiplicity
k
are tagged with
k
-sized vectors of phases

\overline{\alpha}=\alpha_{1}::\dots::\alpha_{k}
.

Wires of multiplicity zero are equivalent to the empty mapping.
We may omit writing the wire multiplicity if it can be deduced by context.

The extension defines two additional generators; a
split
node to split
registers into multiple wires, and a function arrow to apply arbitrary functions
over a register. In this work we restrict the arrow functions to permutations

\sigma:[0\dots k)\to[0\dots k)
that rearrange the order of the wires.
Using the split node and the wire primitives can derive the rotated version,
which we call a
gather
.

We may also depict composition of gathers as single multi-legged generators.
In an analogous manner, we will use a legless gather
to terminate wires with cardinality zero.
This could be encoded as the zero-multiplicity spider
\scriptstyle{[\,]}
, which represents the empty mapping.

Refer to Appendix
A
for a complete definition
of the rewriting rules and the interpretation of the SZX calculus.
Cf.
[
7
]
for a description of the calculus including the generalized arrow generators.

Carette et al.
[
7
]
showed that the SZX calculus
can encode the repetition of a function
f:1_{n}\to 1_{n}
an arbitrary number of times
k\geq 1
as follows:

As an example, given a list
N=[n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}]
and a starting accumulator value
x_{0}
,
this construction would produce the mapping
([n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}],x_{0})\mapsto([m_{1},m_{2},m_{3}],x_{3})
where

(m_{i},x_{i})=g(n_{i},x_{i-1})
for
i\in[1,3]
.

2.2 SZX diagram families and list instantiation

We introduce the definition of a family of SZX diagrams
D:\mathbb{N}^{k}\to\mathscr{D}

as a function from
k
integer
parameters
to SZX diagrams.
We require the structure of the diagrams to be the same for all elements in the family,
parameters may only alter the wire tags and spider phases.
Partial application is allowed, we write
D(n)
to fix the first parameter of
D
.

Since instantiations of a family share the same structure,
we can compose them in parallel by merging the different values of wire tags and spider phases.
We introduce a shorthand for instantiating a family of diagrams on multiple values
and combining the resulting diagrams in parallel.
This definition is strictly more general than the
thickening endofunctor

presented by Carette et al.
[
7
]
,
which replicates a concrete diagram in parallel.
A
list instantiation
of a family of diagrams
D:\mathbb{N}^{k+1}\to\mathscr{D}
over
a list
N
of integers is written as
(D(n),n\in N)
.
This results in a family with one fewer parameter,
(D(n),n\in N):\mathbb{N}^{k}\to\mathscr{D}
.
We graphically depict a list instantiation as a dashed box in a diagram, as follows.

The definition of the list instantiation operator is given recursively
on the construction of
D
in Figure
1
.
On the diagram wires we use
v(N)
to denote the wire cardinality
\sum_{n\in N}v(n)
,

\overrightarrow{\alpha}(N)
for the concatenation of phase vectors

\overrightarrow{\alpha}(n_{1})::\dots::\overrightarrow{\alpha}(n_{m})
,
and
\sigma(N)
for the composition of permutations
\bigotimes_{n\in N}\sigma(n)
.
In general, a permutation arrow
\sigma(N,v,w)
instantiated in concrete values
can be replaced by a reordering of wires between two gather gates using the rewrite rule
\bf{(p)}
.

D:\mathbb{N}^{k+1}\to\mathscr{D}
,
N=[n_{1},\dots,n_{m}]\in\mathbb{N}^{m}

Where
\sigma(N,v,w)\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{v(N)+w(N)\times v(N)+w(N)}
is the permutation defined as the matrix

\sigma(N,v,w)=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{f}^{N}|\sigma_{g}^{N}\end{pmatrix},\quad\sigma_{f}^{N}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{v(N)+w(N)\times v(N)},\ \sigma_{g}^{N}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{v(N)+w(N)\times w(N)}

\begin{array}[]{llll}\sigma_{f}^{[\,]}=Id_{0}&\sigma_{f}^{n::N^{\prime}}=\begin{pmatrix}Id_{v(n)}&0\\
0&0\\
0&\sigma_{f}^{N^{\prime}}\end{pmatrix}&\sigma_{g}^{[\,]}=Id_{0}&\sigma_{g}^{n::N^{\prime}}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
Id_{w(n)}&0\\
0&\sigma_{g}^{N^{\prime}}\end{pmatrix}\end{array}

Lemma 2.4
.

The list instantiation procedure on an
n
-node diagram family adds

\mathcal{O}(n)
nodes to the original diagram.

3
The
\lambda_{D}
calculus

We first define a base language from which to build our translation. In this section we present the calculus
\lambda_{D}
, as a subset of the strongly normalizing Proto-Quipper-D programs. Terms are inductively defined by:

\displaystyle M,N,L:=\;

\displaystyle x\;|\;C\;|\;\mathtt{R}\;|\;\;\mathtt{U}\;|\;0\;|\;1\;|\;n\;|\;\mathtt{meas}\;|\;\mathtt{new}\;|\lambda x^{S}.M\;|\;M\ N\;|\;\lambda^{\prime}x^{P}.M\;|\;M\ @\ N\;|\;

\displaystyle\star\;|\;M\otimes N\;|\;\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x^{S_{1}}\otimes y^{S_{2}}\allowbreak=\allowbreak M\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak N\;|\;M;N\;|\;

\displaystyle\mathtt{VNil}^{A}\;|\;M::N\;|\;\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x^{S}::y^{\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {S}}\allowbreak=\allowbreak M\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak N

\displaystyle M\square N\;|\;\mathtt{ifz\ }{L}\mathtt{\ then\ }{M}\mathtt{\ else\ }{N}\;|\;\mathtt{for\ }{k^{P}}\mathtt{\ in\ }{M}\mathtt{\ do\ }{N}

Where
C
is a set of implicit bounded recursive primitives used for operating
with vectors and iterating functions.
n\in\mathbb{N}
,
\square\in\{+,-,\times,/,\wedge\}
and
\mathtt{ifz\ }{L}\mathtt{\ then\ }{M}\mathtt{\ else\ }{N}
is the conditional that tests for
zero.

Here
\mathtt{U}
denotes a set of unitary operations and
\mathtt{R}
is a phase shift gate
with a parametrized angle. In this article we fix the former to the CNOT and
Hadamard (H) gates, and the latter to the arbitrary rotation gates

R_{z(\alpha)}
and
R_{x(\alpha)}
.

For the remaining constants,
0
and
1
represent bits,
\mathtt{new}
is used to
create a qubit, and
\mathtt{meas}
to measure it.
\star
is the inhabitant of the

\mathtt{Unit}
type, and the sequence
M;N
is used to discard it. Qubits can be
combined via the tensor product
M\otimes N
with
\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x^{S_{1}}\otimes y^{S_{2}}\allowbreak=\allowbreak M\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak N
as its corresponding destructor.

The system supports lists;
\mathtt{VNil}^{A}
represents the empty list,
M::N
the
constructor and
\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x^{S}::y^{\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {S}}\allowbreak=\allowbreak M\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak N
acts as the destructor.
Finally, the term
\mathtt{for\ }{k^{P}}\mathtt{\ in\ }{M}\mathtt{\ do\ }{N}
allows iterating over parameter lists.

The typing system is defined in Figure
2
. We
write
|\Phi|
for the list of variables in a typing context
\Phi
. The type

\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {A}
represents a vector of known length
n
of elements of type
A
.

We differentiate between
state contexts
(Noted with
\Gamma
and

\Delta
) and
parameter contexts
(Noted with
\Phi
). For our case of
study, parameter contexts consist only of pairs
x:{\rm Nature}
or

x:\mathtt{Vec}\ {(n:{\rm Nature})}\ {{\rm Nature}}
, since they are the only non-linear types of variables
that we manage. Every other variable falls under the state context. The terms

\lambda x^{S}.M
and
MN
correspond to the abstraction and application which
will be used for state-typed terms. The analogous constructions for
parameter-typed terms are
\lambda^{\prime}x^{P}.M
and
M@N
.

In this sense we deviate from the original Proto-Quipper-D type system, which
supports a single context decorated with indices. Instead, we use a linear and
non-linear approach similar to the work of Cervesato and
Pfenning
[
10
]
.

A key difference between Quipper (and, by extension, Proto-Quipper-D) and

\lambda_{D}
is the approach to defining circuits. In Quipper, circuits are an
intrinsic part of the language and can be operated upon. In our case, the
translation into SZX diagrams will be mediated with a function defined outside
the language.

Types:

A:=S\;|\;P\;|\;(n:{\rm Nature})\to A[n]

State types:

S:=\mathtt{B}\;|\;\mathtt{Q}\;|\;\mathtt{Unit}\;|\;S_{1}\otimes S_{2}\;|\;S_{1}\multimap S_{2}\;|\;\mathtt{Vec}\ {(n:{\rm Nature})}\ {S}

Parameter types:

P:={\rm Nature}\;|\;\mathtt{Vec}\ {(n:{\rm Nature})}\ {{\rm Nature}}

State contexts:

\Gamma,\Delta:=\cdot\;|\;x:S,\Gamma

Parameter contexts:

\Phi:=\cdot\;|\;x:P,\Phi

\Phi,x:A\vdash x:A\qquad\Phi\vdash 0:\mathtt{B}\qquad\Phi\vdash 1:\mathtt{B}\qquad

\Phi\vdash n:{\rm Nature}n\in\mathbb{N}\qquad\Phi\vdash M\square N:{\rm Nature}\lx@proof@logical@and\Phi\vdash M:{\rm Nature}\Phi\vdash N:{\rm Nature}

\Phi\vdash\mathtt{meas}:\mathtt{Q}\multimap\mathtt{B}\qquad\Phi\vdash\mathtt{new}:\mathtt{B}\multimap\mathtt{Q}\qquad\Phi\vdash\star:\mathtt{Unit}

\Phi\vdash\mathtt{U}:\mathtt{Q}^{\otimes n}\multimap\mathtt{Q}^{\otimes n}\qquad\Phi\vdash\mathtt{R}:(n:{\rm Nature})\to\mathtt{Q}^{\otimes n}\multimap\mathtt{Q}^{\otimes n}

\Phi,\Gamma\vdash\lambda x.M:A\multimap B\Phi,\Gamma,x:A\vdash M:B\qquad\Phi,\Gamma\vdash\lambda^{\prime}x.M:(n:{\rm Nature})\to B\Phi,x:{\rm Nature},\Gamma\vdash M:B[x]

\Phi,\Gamma,\Delta\vdash MN:B\lx@proof@logical@and\Phi,\Gamma\vdash M:A\multimap B\Phi,\Delta\vdash N:A\qquad\Phi,\Gamma\vdash M@N:B[n/N]\lx@proof@logical@and\Phi,\Gamma\vdash M:(n:{\rm Nature})\to B\Phi\vdash N:{\rm Nature}

\Phi,\Gamma,\Delta\vdash M;N:B\lx@proof@logical@and\Phi,\Gamma\vdash M:\mathtt{Unit}\Phi,\Delta\vdash N:B\qquad\Phi,\Gamma,\Delta\vdash M;_{v}N:B\lx@proof@logical@and\Phi,\Gamma\vdash M:\mathtt{Vec}\ {0}\ {A}\Phi,\Delta\vdash N:B

\Phi,\Gamma,\Delta\vdash M\otimes N:A\otimes B\lx@proof@logical@and\Phi,\Gamma\vdash M:A\Phi,\Delta\vdash N:B\qquad\Phi,\Gamma,\Delta\vdash\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x^{A}\otimes y^{B}\allowbreak=\allowbreak M\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak N:C\lx@proof@logical@and\Phi,\Gamma\vdash M:A\otimes B\Phi,\Delta,x:A,y:B\vdash N:C

\Phi\vdash\mathtt{VNil}^{A}:\mathtt{Vec}\ {0}\ {A}\qquad\Phi,\Gamma,\Delta\vdash M\!::\!N\ :\mathtt{Vec}\ {(n+1)}\ {A}\lx@proof@logical@and\Phi,\Gamma\vdash M:A\Phi,\Delta\vdash N:\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {A}

\Phi,\Gamma,\Delta\vdash\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x^{A}:y^{\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {A}}\allowbreak=\allowbreak M\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak N:C\lx@proof@logical@and\Phi,\Gamma\vdash M:\mathtt{Vec}\ {(n+1)}\ {A}\Phi,\Delta,x:A,y:\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {A}\vdash N:C

\Phi,\Gamma^{n}\vdash\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{V}\mathtt{\ do\ }{M}:\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {A[k]}\lx@proof@logical@and n:{\rm Nature}\Phi\vdash V:\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {{\rm Nature}}k:{\rm Nature},\Phi,\Gamma\vdash M:A[k]

\Phi,\Gamma\vdash\mathtt{ifz\ }{L}\mathtt{\ then\ }{M}\mathtt{\ else\ }{N}:A\lx@proof@logical@and\Phi\vdash L:{\rm Nature}\Phi,\Gamma\vdash M:A\Phi,\Gamma\vdash N:A

Figure 2
:
Type system.

Types are divided into two kinds; parameter and state types. Both of these can
depend on terms of type
{\rm Nature}
. For the scope of this work, this dependence may
only influence the size of vectors types.

Parameter types represent non-linear variable types which are known at the time
of generation of the concrete quantum operations. In the translation into SZX
diagrams, these variables may dictate the labels of the wires and spiders.
Vectors of
{\rm Nature}
terms represent their cartesian product.
On the other hand, state types correspond to the quantum operations and states
to be computed. In the translation, these terms inform the shape and composition
of the diagrams. Vectors of state type terms represent their tensor product.

In lieu of unbounded and implicit recursion, we define a series of primitive
functions for performing explicit vector manipulation. These primitives can be
defined in the original language, with the advantage of them being strongly
normalizing. The first four primitives are used to manage state vectors, while
the last one is used for generating parameters. For ease of translation some
terms are decorated with type annotations, however we will omit these for
clarity when the type is apparent.

\Phi\vdash\mathtt{accuMap}_{A,B,C}:(n:{\rm Nature})\to\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {A}\multimap\;\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {(A\multimap C\multimap B\otimes C)}\multimap C\multimap(\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {B})\otimes C

\Phi\vdash\mathtt{split}_{A}:(n:{\rm Nature})\to(m:{\rm Nature})\to\mathtt{Vec}\ {(n+m)}\ {A}\multimap\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {A}\otimes\mathtt{Vec}\ {m}\ {A}

\Phi\vdash\mathtt{append}_{A}:(n:{\rm Nature})\to(m:{\rm Nature})\to\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {A}\multimap\mathtt{Vec}\ {m}\ {A}\multimap\mathtt{Vec}\ {(n+m)}\ {A}

\Phi\vdash\mathtt{drop}:(n:{\rm Nature})\to\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {\mathtt{Unit}}\multimap\;\mathtt{Unit}

\Phi\vdash\mathtt{range\ }:(n:{\rm Nature})\to(m:{\rm Nature})\to\mathtt{Vec}\ {(m-n)}\ {{\rm Nature}}

Since every diagram represents a linear map between qubits there is no
representation equivalent to non-terminating terms, even for weakly normalizing
programs. This is the main reason behind the design choice of the primitives
set.
We include the operational semantics
of the calculus and primitives in Appendix
B
. The encoding
of the primitives as Proto-Quipper-D functions is shown in
Appendix
C
.

We additionally define the following helpful terms based on the previous
primitives to aid in the manipulation of vectors.
Cf. Appendix
B
for their definition as
\lambda_{D}
-terms.

\Phi\vdash\mathtt{map}_{A,B}:(n:{\rm Nature})\to\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {A}\multimap\;\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {(A\multimap B)}\multimap\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {B}

\Phi\vdash\mathtt{fold}_{A,C}:(n:{\rm Nature})\to\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {A}\multimap\;\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {(A\multimap C\multimap C)}\multimap C\multimap C

\Phi\vdash\mathtt{compose}_{A}:(n:{\rm Nature})\to\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {(A\multimap A)}\multimap A\multimap A

The distinction between primitives that deal with state and parameters highlights the inclusion of the
\mathtt{for}
as a construction into the language instead of a primitive. Since it acts over both parameter and state types, its function is effectively to bridge the gap between the two of them. This operation closely corresponds to the list instantiation procedure presented in the Section
2.1
.

For example, if we take
ns
to be a vector of natural numbers, and
xs
a vector of abstractions
R@k(new0)
. The term
\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{ns}\mathtt{\ do\ }{xs}
generates a vector of quantum maps by instantiating the abstractions for each individual parameter in
ns
.

4
Encoding programs as diagram families

In this section we introduce an encoding of the lambda calculus presented in Section
3

into families of SZX diagrams with context variables as inputs and term values as outputs.
We split the lambda-terms into those that represent linear mappings between quantum states
and can be encoded as families of SZX diagrams, and parameter terms that can be completely evaluated
at compile-time.

4.1 Parameter evaluation

We say a type is
evaluable
if it has the form

A=(n_{1}:{\rm Nature})\to\dots\to(n_{k}:{\rm Nature})\to P[n_{1},\dots,n_{k}]
with
P
a parameter type.
Since
A
does not encode a quantum operation,
we interpret it directly into functions over vectors of natural numbers.
The translation of an evaluable type,
\left\lfloor{A}\right\rfloor
, is defined recursively as follows:

\left\lfloor{(n:{\rm Nature})\to B[n]}\right\rfloor=\mathbb{N}\to\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\left\lfloor{B[n]}\right\rfloor\qquad\left\lfloor{{\rm Nature}}\right\rfloor=\mathbb{N}\qquad\left\lfloor{\mathtt{Vec}\ {(n:{\rm Nature})}\ {{\rm Nature}}}\right\rfloor=\mathbb{N}^{n}

Given a type judgement
\Phi\vdash L:P
where
P
is an evaluable type,
we define
\left\lfloor{L}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}
as the evaluation of the term into a function from parameters into products of natural numbers.
Since the typing is syntax directed, the evaluation is defined directly over the terms as follows:

\left\lfloor{x}\right\rfloor_{x:{\rm Nature},\Phi}=x,|\Phi|\mapsto x\qquad\left\lfloor{n}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=|\Phi|\mapsto n\qquad\left\lfloor{M\square N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\square\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)

\left\lfloor{M\ ::\ N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\times\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\qquad\left\lfloor{\mathtt{VNil}^{\rm Nature}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=|\Phi|\mapsto[]

\left\lfloor{\lambda^{\prime}x^{P}.M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=x,|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(x,|\Phi|)\qquad\left\lfloor{M@N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|),\Phi)

\left\lfloor{\mathtt{ifz\ }{L}\mathtt{\ then\ }{M}\mathtt{\ else\ }{N}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=|\Phi|\mapsto\begin{cases}\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\text{ if }\left\lfloor{L}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)=0\\
\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\text{ otherwise}\end{cases}\quad\left\lfloor{\mathtt{range\ }}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=n,m,|\Phi|\mapsto\bigtimes_{i=n}^{m-1}i

\left\lfloor{\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{V}\mathtt{\ do\ }{M}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=|\Phi|\mapsto\bigtimes_{k\in\left\lfloor{V}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)}\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{k:{\rm Nature}\Phi}(k,|\Phi|)

\left\lfloor{\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x^{P}::y^{\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {P}}\allowbreak=\allowbreak M\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{x:P,y:\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {P},\Phi}(y_{1},[y_{2},\dots,y_{n}],|\Phi|){\scriptstyle{\text{ where }[y_{1},\dots,y_{n}]=\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)}}

Lemma 4.1
.

Given an evaluable type
A
and a type judgement
\Phi\vdash L:A
,

\left\lfloor{L}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}\in\bigtimes_{x:P\in\Phi}\left\lfloor{P}\right\rfloor\to\left\lfloor{A}\right\rfloor
.

Lemma 4.2
.

Given an evaluable type
A
,
a type judgement
\Phi\vdash L:A
, and
M\to N
, then
\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}
.

4.2 Diagram encoding

A non-evaluable type has necessarily the form
A=(n_{1}:{\rm Nature})\to\dots\to(n_{k}:{\rm Nature})\to S
,
with
S
any state type.
We call such types
translatable
since they correspond to terms that
encode quantum operations that can be described as families of diagrams.

We first define a translation
\left\llbracket{\cdot}\right\rrbracket
from state types
into wire multiplicities as follows.
Notice that due to the symmetries of the SZX diagrams
the linear functions have the same representation as the products.

\left\llbracket{\mathtt{B}}\right\rrbracket=1\qquad\left\llbracket{\mathtt{Q}}\right\rrbracket=1\qquad\left\llbracket{\mathtt{Vec}\ {(n:{\rm Nature})}\ {A}}\right\rrbracket=\left\llbracket{A}\right\rrbracket^{\otimes n}\qquad\left\llbracket{A\otimes B}\right\rrbracket=\left\llbracket{A}\right\rrbracket\otimes\left\llbracket{B}\right\rrbracket\qquad\left\llbracket{A\multimap B}\right\rrbracket=\left\llbracket{A}\right\rrbracket\otimes\left\llbracket{B}\right\rrbracket

Given a translatable type judgement

\Phi,\Gamma\vdash M:(n_{1}:{\rm Nature})\to\dots\to(n_{k}:{\rm Nature})\to S

we can encode it as a family of SZX diagrams

where
\delta
is the Kronecker delta and
l=\left\lfloor{L}\right\rfloor(|\Phi|)
. Notice that
the
\mathtt{new}
and
\mathtt{meas}
operations share the same translation. Although
\mathtt{new}

can be encoded as a simple wire, we keep the additional node to maintain the
symmetry with the measurement.

The unitary operators
U
and rotations
R
correspond to a predefined set of primitives,
and their translation is defined on a by case basis.
The following table shows the encoding of the operators used in this paper.

Name

The primitives
\mathtt{split}
,
\mathtt{append}
,
\mathtt{drop}
and
\mathtt{accuMap}
are translated below.
Since vectors are isomorphic to products in the wire encoding,
the first three primitives do not perform any operation.
For the accumulating map we utilize the construction presented in Lemma
2.1
,
replacing the function box with a function vector input.

to a single wire on the right of the diagram for clarity.

where
\tau_{n,A,B,C}
is a permutation that rearranges the vectors of functions into tensors of
vectors for each parameter and return value.
That is,
\tau_{n,A,B,C}
reorders a sequence of registers
(A,C,B,C)\dots(A,C,B,C)

into the sequence
(A\dots A)(C\dots C)(B\dots B)(C\dots C)
.
It is defined as follows,

\tau_{n,A,B,C}(i)=\begin{cases}{i}\ \text{mod}\ {k}+a*({i}\ \text{div}\ {k})&\text{if }{i}\ \text{mod}\ {k}<a\\
{i}\ \text{mod}\ {k}+c*({i}\ \text{div}\ {k})+a*(n-1)&\text{if }a\leq{i}\ \text{mod}\ {k}<(a+c)\\
{i}\ \text{mod}\ {k}+b*({i}\ \text{div}\ {k})+(a+c)*(n-1)&\text{if }(a+c)\leq{i}\ \text{mod}\ {k}<(a+c+b)\\
{i}\ \text{mod}\ {k}+c*({i}\ \text{div}\ {k})+(a+c+b)*(n-1)&\text{if }(a+c+b)\leq{i}\ \text{mod}\ {k}\\
\end{cases}

for
i\in[0,(a+c+b+c)*n)
,
where mod and div are the integer modulo and division operators,

a=\left\llbracket{A}\right\rrbracket
,
b=\left\llbracket{B}\right\rrbracket
,
c=\left\llbracket{C}\right\rrbracket
,
and
k=a+c+b+c
.

As a consequence of Lemma
2.4
,
the number of nodes in the produced diagrams grows linearly
with the size of the input.
Notice that the ZX spiders, the ground, and the Hadamard operator
are only produced in the translations of the quantum primitives.
We may instead have used other variations of the calculus
supporting the scalable extension, such as the ZH calculus
[
3
]
,
better suited for other sets of quantum operators.

Lemma 4.3
.

The translation procedure is correct in respect to the operational semantics of
\lambda_{D}
.
If
A
is a translatable type,
\Phi,\Gamma\vdash M:A
, and
M\to N
,
then
\left\llbracket{M}\right\rrbracket_{\Phi,\Gamma}=\left\llbracket{N}\right\rrbracket_{\Phi,\Gamma}
.

5
Application example: QFT

The Quantum Fourier Transform is an algorithm used extensively in quantum computation,
notably as part of Shor’s algorithm for integer factorization
[
17
]
.
The QFT function operates generically over
n
-qubit states and in general a circuit encoding of it
requires
\mathcal{O}(n^{2})
gates.
In this section we present an encoding of the algorithm as a
\lambda_{D}
term,
followed by the translation into a family of constant-sized diagrams.
The corresponding Proto-Quipper-D program is listed in Appendix
D
.

The following presentation divides the algorithm into three parts.
The
crot
term applies a controlled rotation over a qubit with a parametrized angle.

apply_crot
operates over the last
n-k
qubits of an
n
-qubit state
by applying a Hadamard gate to the first one and then using it as target
of successive
crot
applications using the rest of the qubits as controls.
Finally,
qft
repeats
apply_crot
for all values of
k
.
In the terms, we use
n\dots m
as a shorthand for
\mathtt{range\ }\ @n\ @m
.

\text{crot}:(n:{\rm Nature})\to(\mathtt{Q}\otimes\mathtt{Q})\multimap(\mathtt{Q}\otimes\mathtt{Q})

\text{crot}:=\lambda^{\prime}n^{{\rm Nature}}.\lambda qs^{\mathtt{Q}\otimes\mathtt{Q}}.\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak c^{\mathtt{Q}}\otimes q^{\mathtt{Q}}\allowbreak=\allowbreak qs\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak c^{\mathtt{Q}}\otimes q^{\mathtt{Q}}\allowbreak=\allowbreak\mathtt{CNOT}\ c\ (\mathtt{Rz}\ @2^{n}\ q)\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak\mathtt{CNOT}\ c\ (\mathtt{Rz^{-1}}\ @2^{n}\ q)

\text{apply\_crot}:(n:{\rm Nature})\to(k:{\rm Nature})\to\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {\mathtt{Q}}\multimap\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {\mathtt{Q}}

\displaystyle\text{apply\_crot}:=\

\displaystyle\lambda^{\prime}n^{\rm Nature}.\ \lambda^{\prime}k^{\rm Nature}.\ \lambda qs^{\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {\mathtt{Q}}}.

\displaystyle\mathtt{ifz\ }{(n-k)}\mathtt{\ then\ }{qs}\mathtt{\ else\ }{}

\displaystyle\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak h^{\mathtt{Vec}\ {k}\ {\mathtt{Q}}}\otimes qs^{\prime\ \mathtt{Vec}\ {n-k}\ {\mathtt{Q}}}\allowbreak=\allowbreak\mathtt{split}\ @k\ @(n-k)\ qs\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak

\displaystyle\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak q^{\mathtt{Q}}\otimes cs^{\mathtt{Vec}\ {n-k-1}\ {\mathtt{Q}}}\allowbreak=\allowbreak qs^{\prime}\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak

\displaystyle\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak fs^{\mathtt{Vec}\ {(n-k-1)}\ {(\mathtt{Q}\otimes\mathtt{Q}\multimap\mathtt{Q}\otimes\mathtt{Q})}}\allowbreak=\allowbreak\mathtt{for\ }{m^{\rm Nature}}\mathtt{\ in\ }{2..(n-k+1)}\mathtt{\ do\ }{\text{crot }@m}\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak\!\!

\displaystyle\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak cs^{\prime\ (\mathtt{Vec}\ {n-k-1}\ {\mathtt{Q}})}\otimes q^{\prime\ \mathtt{Q}}\allowbreak=\allowbreak\mathtt{accuMap}\ fs\ (H\ q)\ cs\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak

\displaystyle\text{concat }h\ (q^{\prime}:cs^{\prime})

\text{qft}:(n:{\rm Nature})\to\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {\mathtt{Q}}\multimap\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {\mathtt{Q}}

\displaystyle\text{qft}:=\

\displaystyle\lambda^{\prime}n^{\rm Nature}.\lambda qs^{\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {\mathtt{Q}}}.\mathtt{compose}

\displaystyle(\mathtt{for\ }{k^{\rm Nature}}\mathtt{\ in\ }{\text{reverse\_vec }@(0..n)}\mathtt{\ do\ }{\lambda qs^{\prime\ \mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {\mathtt{Q}}}.\text{apply\_crot }@n\ @k\ qs^{\prime}})\ qs

The translation of each term into a family of diagrams is shown below.
We omit the wire connecting the function inputs to the right side
of the graphs for clarity and eliminate superfluous gathers and splitters
using rules
\mathbf{(sg)}
and
\mathbf{(gs)}
.
Notice that, in contrast to a quantum circuit encoding,
the resulting diagram’s size does not depend on the number of qubits
n
.

6
Discussion

In this article, we presented an efficient method to compile
parametric quantum programs written in a fragment of the Proto-Quipper-D
language into families of SZX diagrams.
We restricted the fragment to strongly normalizing terms that can be represented
as diagrams.
Additionally, we introduced a notation to easily compose elements of a diagram
family in parallel.
We proved that our method produces compact diagrams
and shown that it can encode non-trivial algorithms.

A current line of work is defining categorical semantics for the calculus and
families of diagrams, including a subsequent proof of adequacy for the
translation. More work needs to be done to expand the fragment of the Quipper
language that can be translated.

We would like to acknowledge Benoît Valiron for helpful discussion on this
topic, and Frank Fu for his help during the implementation of the
Proto-Quipper-D primitives. This work was supported in part by the French
National Research Agency (ANR) under the research projects SoftQPRO
ANR-17-CE25-0009-02 and Plan France 2030 ANR-22-PETQ-0007, by the DGE of the
French Ministry of Industry under the research project PIA-GDN/QuantEx
P163746-484124, by the project STIC-AmSud project Qapla’ 21-SITC-10, the
ECOS-Sud A17C03 project, the PICT-2019-1272 project, the French-Argentinian IRP SINFIN
and the PIP 11220200100368CO project.

Appendix B
Operational Semantics of the
\lambda_{D}
calculus

We define a weak call-by-value small step operational semantics on Table
1
.

\displaystyle V:=\;

\displaystyle x\;|\;C\;|\;0\;|\;1\;|\;\mathtt{meas}\;|\;\mathtt{new}\;|\;\mathtt{U}\;|\;

\displaystyle\lambda x^{S}.M\;|\;\lambda^{\prime}x^{P}.M\;|\star\;|\;M\otimes N\;|\;

\displaystyle\mathtt{VNil}\;|\;M::N\;

\displaystyle(\lambda x.M)V

\displaystyle\to M[V/x]

\displaystyle(\lambda^{\prime}x.M)@V

\displaystyle\to M[V/x]

\displaystyle\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x\otimes y\allowbreak=\allowbreak M_{1}\otimes M_{2}\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak N

\displaystyle\to N[x/M_{1}][y/M_{2}]

\displaystyle\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x::y\allowbreak=\allowbreak M_{1}::M_{2}\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak N

\displaystyle\to N[x/M_{1}][y/M_{2}]

\displaystyle\mathtt{ifz\ }{V}\mathtt{\ then\ }{M}\mathtt{\ else\ }{N}

\displaystyle\to\begin{cases}M\qquad\text{If }V=0\\
N\qquad\text{Otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle\star\ ;\ M

\displaystyle\to M

\displaystyle\mathtt{VNil}\ ;_{v}\ M

\displaystyle\to M

\displaystyle V_{1}\square V_{2}

\displaystyle\to V\qquad\text{Where }V_{i}=n_{i}\text{ and }V=n_{1}\square n_{2}

\displaystyle\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{M_{1}\ ::M_{2}}\mathtt{\ do\ }{N}

\displaystyle\to N[k/M_{1}]\ ::\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{M_{2}}\mathtt{\ do\ }{N}

\displaystyle\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{\mathtt{VNil}}\mathtt{\ do\ }{N}

\displaystyle\to\mathtt{VNil}

MV\to NVM\to N\qquad LM\to LNM\to N\qquad M@V\to N@VM\to N\qquad L@M\to L@NM\to N

\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x\otimes y\allowbreak=\allowbreak M\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak L\to\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x\otimes y\allowbreak=\allowbreak N\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak LM\to N\qquad\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x::y\allowbreak=\allowbreak M\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak L\to\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x::y\allowbreak=\allowbreak N\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak LM\to N

L\square M\to L\square NM\to N\qquad M\square V\to M\square VM\to N

M\ ;\ L\to N\ ;\ LM\to N\qquad\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x:y\allowbreak=\allowbreak M\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak L\to\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x:y\allowbreak=\allowbreak N\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak LM\to N

\mathtt{ifz\ }{M}\mathtt{\ then\ }{L_{1}}\mathtt{\ else\ }{L_{2}}\to\mathtt{ifz\ }{N}\mathtt{\ then\ }{L_{1}}\mathtt{\ else\ }{L_{2}}M\to N\qquad\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{M}\mathtt{\ do\ }{L}\to\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{N}\mathtt{\ do\ }{L}M\to N

Table 1
:
Rewrite system for
\lambda_{D}
.

A key point to note here is that every rewriting rule preserves the state. There are no measurements or unitary operations applied, the rewriting is merely syntactical. Since our goal is translation into an SZX-diagram, this system is powerful enough. We include the rewrite rules for the primitives on Table
2
.

\displaystyle\mathtt{accuMap}\ @n\ xs\ fs\ z\to

\displaystyle\mathtt{ifz\ }{n}\mathtt{\ then\ }{xs\ ;_{v}\ fs\ ;_{v}\ \mathtt{VNil}\otimes z}\mathtt{\ else\ }{}

\displaystyle\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x::xs^{\prime}\allowbreak=\allowbreak xs\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak f::fs^{\prime}\allowbreak=\allowbreak fs\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak

\displaystyle\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak y\otimes z^{\prime}\allowbreak=\allowbreak f\ x\ z\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak ys\otimes z^{\prime\prime}\allowbreak=\allowbreak\mathtt{accuMap}\ @(n-1)\ xs^{\prime}\ fs^{\prime}\ z^{\prime}\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak

\displaystyle(y::ys)\otimes z^{\prime\prime}

\displaystyle\mathtt{split}\ @n\ @m\ xs\to

\displaystyle\mathtt{ifz\ }{n}\mathtt{\ then\ }{\mathtt{VNil}\otimes xs}\mathtt{\ else\ }{}\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak y::xs^{\prime}\allowbreak=\allowbreak xs\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak

\displaystyle\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak ys_{1}\otimes ys_{2}\allowbreak=\allowbreak\mathtt{split}@(n-1)\ @m\ xs^{\prime}\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak(y::ys_{1})\otimes ys_{2}

\displaystyle\mathtt{append}\ @n\ @m\ xs\ ys\to

\displaystyle\mathtt{ifz\ }{n}\mathtt{\ then\ }{xs\ ;_{v}\ ys}\mathtt{\ else\ }{}

\displaystyle\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x::xs^{\prime}\allowbreak=\allowbreak xs\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak x::(\mathtt{append}\ @(n-1)\ @m\ xs^{\prime}\ ys)

\displaystyle\mathtt{drop}\ @n\ xs\to

\displaystyle\mathtt{ifz\ }{n}\mathtt{\ then\ }{xs\ ;_{v}\ \star}\mathtt{\ else\ }{\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x::xs^{\prime}\allowbreak=\allowbreak xs\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak x\ ;\ \mathtt{drop}\ @(n-1)\ xs^{\prime}}

\displaystyle\mathtt{range\ }\ @n\ @m\to

\displaystyle\mathtt{ifz\ }{m-n}\mathtt{\ then\ }{\mathtt{VNil}}\mathtt{\ else\ }{n\ ::\mathtt{range\ }\ @(n+1)\ @m}

:
Reductions pertaining to the primitives.

. They provide syntactic sugar to deal with state vectors.

\displaystyle\mathtt{in\ let}\ {us\otimes r}=\mathtt{accuMap}\ @n\ xs\ fs^{\prime}\ z

.

​

2.1
)

Let
g:1_{n}\otimes 1_{s}\to 1_{m}\otimes 1_{s}
and

Proof
.

Notice that any wire in the initialized diagrams has cardinality zero.
By rules
{(\bf\emptyset 1)}
,
{(\bf\emptyset 2)}
,
{(\bf\emptyset 3)}
,

{(\bf\emptyset 4)}
, and
{(\bf\emptyset w)}

every internal node can be eliminated from the diagram.

\square

Lemma
.

​
(
2.4
)

The list instantiation procedure on an
n
-node diagram family adds

\mathcal{O}(n)
nodes to the original diagram.

Proof
.

By induction on the term construction.
Notice that the instantiation of any term except the gather
does not introduce any new nodes, and the gather introduction
creates exactly one extra node.
Therefore, the list instantiation adds a number of nodes equal to
the number of gather generators in the diagram.

\square

Lemma E.1
.

Given type judgements
\Phi,x:A\vdash M:B
, and
\Phi\vdash N:A
.
\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{x:A,\Phi}(\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi},|\Phi|)=\left\lfloor{M[N/x]}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(

|\Phi|

)
.

Proof
.

Proof by straightforward induction on
M
.

\square

Lemma
.

​
(
4.1
)

Given an evaluable type
A
and a type judgement
\Phi\vdash M:A
,

\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}\in\bigtimes_{x:P\in\Phi}\left\lfloor{P}\right\rfloor\to\left\lfloor{A}\right\rfloor
.

Proof
.

By induction on the typing judgement
\Phi\vdash M:A
:

•

If
\Phi\vdash n:{\rm Nature}
, then
\left\lfloor{n}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=|\Phi|\mapsto n\in\bigtimes_{x:P\in\Phi}\left\lfloor{P}\right\rfloor\to\mathbb{N}
.

•

If
\Phi,x:A\vdash x:A
, then
\left\lfloor{x}\right\rfloor_{x:A,\Phi}=x,|\Phi|\mapsto x\in\bigtimes_{y:P\in x:A,\Phi}\left\lfloor{P}\right\rfloor\to\left\lfloor{A}\right\rfloor
.

•

If
\Phi\vdash M\square N:{\rm Nature}\Phi,\Gamma,\Delta\vdash M\!::\!N\ :\mathtt{Vec}\ {(n+1)}\ {A}
, then
\left\lfloor{M\square N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\square

\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(

|\Phi|

)
. By inductive hypothesis,
\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|),\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\in\mathbb{N}
. Then,

|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\square\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\in\bigtimes_{x:P\in\Phi}\left\lfloor{P}\right\rfloor\to\mathbb{N}
.

•

If
\Phi\vdash\lambda^{\prime}x.M:(x:P)\to B
then
\left\lfloor{\lambda^{\prime}x^{P}.M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=x,|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(x,|\Phi|)
. By inductive hypothesis,
\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(x,|\Phi|)\in\left\lfloor{B}\right\rfloor
. Then,
|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(x,|\Phi|)\in\bigtimes_{y:P\in x:P\Phi}\left\lfloor{P}\right\rfloor\to\left\lfloor{B}\right\rfloor
.

•

If
\Phi,\Gamma\vdash M@N:B[x/r]
, then
\left\lfloor{M@N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|),\Phi)
. By inductive hypothesis,
\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\in\mathbb{N}
and
x\mapsto\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(x,\Phi)\in\left\lfloor{x:{\rm Nature}\to B[x]}\right\rfloor
. Then,
|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|),\Phi)\in\bigtimes_{y:P\in\Phi}\left\lfloor{P}\right\rfloor\to\left\lfloor{B[A/x]}\right\rfloor
.

•

If
\Phi\vdash\mathtt{VNil}^{A}:\mathtt{Vec}\ {0}\ {A}
, then
\left\lfloor{\mathtt{VNil}^{P}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=|\Phi|\mapsto[]\in\bigtimes_{x:P\in\Phi}\left\lfloor{P}\right\rfloor\to\mathbb{N}^{0}
.

•

If
\Phi,\Gamma,\Delta\vdash M\!::\!N\ :\mathtt{Vec}\ {(n+1)}\ {A}
, then
\left\lfloor{M\ ::\ N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\times\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)
. By inductive hypothesis
{M}_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\in\left\lfloor{A}\right\rfloor
and
\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\in\left\lfloor{A}\right\rfloor^{n}
. Then,
|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\times\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\in\bigtimes_{x:P\in\Phi}\left\lfloor{P}\right\rfloor\to\left\lfloor{A}\right\rfloor^{n+1}
.

•

If
\Phi,\Gamma\vdash\mathtt{ifz\ }{L}\mathtt{\ then\ }{M}\mathtt{\ else\ }{N}:A
, then

\left\lfloor{\mathtt{ifz\ }{L}\mathtt{\ then\ }{M}\mathtt{\ else\ }{N}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=|\Phi|\mapsto\begin{cases}\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\text{ if }\left\lfloor{L}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)=0\\
\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\text{ otherwise}\end{cases}.

By inductive hypothesis
\left\lfloor{m}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|),\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\in\left\lfloor{A}\right\rfloor
and
\left\lfloor{L}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\in\mathbb{N}
.

Then
\left\lfloor{\mathtt{ifz\ }{L}\mathtt{\ then\ }{M}\mathtt{\ else\ }{N}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}\in\bigtimes_{x:P\in\Phi}\left\lfloor{P}\right\rfloor\to\left\lfloor{A}\right\rfloor
.

•

If
\Phi\vdash\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{N}\mathtt{\ do\ }{M}:\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {A}
, then

\left\lfloor{\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{V}\mathtt{\ do\ }{M}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=|\Phi|\mapsto\bigtimes_{k\in\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)}\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{k:{\rm Nature}\Phi}(k,

|\Phi|)
.
By induction hypothesis,
\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\in{\rm Nature}^{n}
and

x\mapsto\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(x,\Phi)\in\left\lfloor{k:{\rm Nature}\to A[k]}\right\rfloor
. Then
|\Phi|\mapsto\bigtimes_{k\in\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)}\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{k:{\rm Nature}\Phi}(k,|\Phi|)\in\bigtimes_{x:P\in\Phi}\left\lfloor{P}\right\rfloor\to\left\lfloor{A[k/N]}\right\rfloor^{n}
.

•

If
\Phi\vdash\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x^{B}:y^{\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {B}}\allowbreak=\allowbreak M\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak N:A
, then

\left\lfloor{\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x^{P}::y^{\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {P}}\allowbreak=\allowbreak M\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=
|\Phi|\mapsto

\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{x:P,y:\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {P}\Phi}(y_{1},[y_{2},\dots,y_{n}],|\Phi|)

where
[y_{1},\dots,y_{n}]=\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)
.

By inductive hypothesis

\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\in\left\lfloor{B}\right\rfloor^{n}
and
\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{x:P,y:\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {P}\Phi}(y_{1},[y_{2},\dots,y_{n}],|\Phi|)\in\left\lfloor{A}\right\rfloor
. Then
|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{x:P,y:\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {P}\Phi}(y_{1},[y_{2},\dots,y_{n}],|\Phi|)\in\bigtimes_{x:P\in\Phi}\left\lfloor{P}\right\rfloor\to\left\lfloor{A}\right\rfloor
.

•

If
\Phi\vdash\mathtt{range\ }:(n:{\rm Nature})\to(m:{\rm Nature})\to\mathtt{Vec}\ {(m-n)}\ {{\rm Nature}}
, then
\left\lfloor{\mathtt{range\ }}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=n,m,|\Phi|\mapsto\bigtimes_{i=n}^{m-1}i\in\bigtimes_{z:P\in x:{\rm Nature},y:{\rm Nature},\Phi}\left\lfloor{P}\right\rfloor\to\mathbb{N}^{m-n}

\square

Lemma
.

​
(
4.2
)

Given an evaluable type
A
,
a type judgement
\Phi\vdash M:A
, and
M\to N
, then
\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}
.

Proof
.

By induction on the evaluation function
\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}
:

•

If
M=x
,
M=n
,
M=\mathtt{VNil}^{\rm Nature}
,
M=\lambda^{\prime}x.M^{\prime}
,
M=M_{1}\ ::\ M_{2}
or
M=\mathtt{range\ }
then
M
is in normal form and it does not reduce.

•

If
M=M_{1}\square M_{2}
we have three cases:

–

If
M\to M_{1}\square N
with
M_{2}\to N
, then:

\displaystyle\left\lfloor{M_{1}\square M_{2}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M_{1}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\square\left\lfloor{M_{2}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M_{1}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\square\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=\left\lfloor{M_{1}\square N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

–

If
M\to N\square V
with
M_{1}\to N
, then:

\displaystyle\left\lfloor{M_{1}\square V}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M_{1}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\square\left\lfloor{V}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\square\left\lfloor{V}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=\left\lfloor{N\square V}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

–

If
M\to n
with
M_{i}=n_{i}\in\mathbb{N}
and
n=n_{1}\square n_{2}
, then:

\displaystyle\left\lfloor{n_{1}\square n_{2}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{n_{1}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\square\left\lfloor{n_{2}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto n_{1}\square n_{2}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto n

\displaystyle=\left\lfloor{n}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

•

If
M=M_{1}\ @\ M_{2}
we have three cases:

–

If
M\to M_{1}\ @\ N
with
M_{2}\to N
, then:

\displaystyle\left\lfloor{M_{1}\ @\ M_{2}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M_{1}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(\left\lfloor{M_{2}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|),\Phi)

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M_{1}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|),\Phi)

\displaystyle=\left\lfloor{M_{1}\ @\ N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

–

If
M\to N\ @\ V
with
M_{1}\to N
, then:

\displaystyle\left\lfloor{M_{1}\ @\ V}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M_{1}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(\left\lfloor{V}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|),\Phi)

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M_{1}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(\left\lfloor{V}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|),\Phi)

\displaystyle=\left\lfloor{N\ @V}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

–

If
M\to M^{\prime}[V/x]
with
M_{1}=\lambda^{\prime}x.M^{\prime}
and
M_{2}=V
, then:

\displaystyle\left\lfloor{(\lambda^{\prime}x.M)@V}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{\lambda^{\prime}x.M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(\left\lfloor{V}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|),\Phi)

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto(x,|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{x,\Phi}(x,|\Phi|))(\left\lfloor{V}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|),\Phi)

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M[V/X]}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=\left\lfloor{M[V/X]}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

•

If
M=\mathtt{ifz\ }{M^{\prime}}\mathtt{\ then\ }{L}\mathtt{\ else\ }{R}
we have three cases:

–

If
M\to\mathtt{ifz\ }{N}\mathtt{\ then\ }{L}\mathtt{\ else\ }{R}
with
M^{\prime}\to N
, then:

\displaystyle\left\lfloor{\mathtt{ifz\ }{M^{\prime}}\mathtt{\ then\ }{L}\mathtt{\ else\ }{R}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\begin{cases}\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\text{ if }\left\lfloor{M^{\prime}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)=0\\
\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\text{ otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\begin{cases}\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\text{ if }\left\lfloor{M^{\prime}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)=0\\
\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\text{ otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle=\left\lfloor{\mathtt{ifz\ }{N}\mathtt{\ then\ }{L}\mathtt{\ else\ }{R}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

–

If
M\to L
with
M^{\prime}=0
, then:

\displaystyle\left\lfloor{\mathtt{ifz\ }{M^{\prime}}\mathtt{\ then\ }{L}\mathtt{\ else\ }{R}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\begin{cases}\left\lfloor{M}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\text{ if }\left\lfloor{M^{\prime}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)=0\\
\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\text{ otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{L}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=\left\lfloor{L}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

–

The symmetric case for the else branch is similar to the previous one.

•

If
M=\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{M^{\prime}}\mathtt{\ do\ }{R}
we have three cases:

–

If
M\to\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{N}\mathtt{\ do\ }{R}
with
M^{\prime}\to N
, then:

\displaystyle\left\lfloor{\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{M^{\prime}}\mathtt{\ do\ }{R}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\bigtimes_{k\in\left\lfloor{M^{\prime}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)}\left\lfloor{R}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(k,|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\bigtimes_{k\in\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)}\left\lfloor{R}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(k,|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=\left\lfloor{\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{N}\mathtt{\ do\ }{R}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

–

If
M\to R[k/M_{1}]\ :\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{M_{2}}\mathtt{\ do\ }{R}
with
M^{\prime}=V::L
, then:

\displaystyle\left\lfloor{\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{M_{1}\ ::\ M_{2}}\mathtt{\ do\ }{R}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\bigtimes_{k\in\left\lfloor{M_{1}\ ::\ M_{2}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)}\left\lfloor{R}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(k,|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\bigtimes_{k\in\left\lfloor{M_{1}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)\times\left\lfloor{M_{2}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)}\left\lfloor{R}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(k,|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{R}\right\rfloor_{k,\Phi}(\left\lfloor{M_{1}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|),|\Phi|)\times\bigtimes_{k\in\left\lfloor{M_{2}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|}\left\lfloor{R}\right\rfloor_{k,\Phi}(k,|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=\left\lfloor{R[M_{1}/k]}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}\times\left\lfloor{\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{M_{2}}\mathtt{\ do\ }{R}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

\displaystyle=\left\lfloor{R[M_{1}/k]\ ::\ \mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{M_{2}}\mathtt{\ do\ }{R}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

–

If
M\to\mathtt{VNil}
with
M^{\prime}=\mathtt{VNil}^{\rm Nature}
, then:

\displaystyle\left\lfloor{\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{\mathtt{VNil}^{\rm Nature}}\mathtt{\ do\ }{R}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\bigtimes_{k\in\left\lfloor{\mathtt{VNil}^{\rm Nature}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)}\left\lfloor{R}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(k,|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\bigtimes_{k\in[]}\left\lfloor{R}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(k,|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto[]

\displaystyle=\left\lfloor{\mathtt{VNil}^{\rm Nature}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

•

If
M=\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x::y\allowbreak=\allowbreak M_{1}\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak M_{2}
we have two cases:

–

If
M\to\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x::y\allowbreak=\allowbreak N\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak M_{2}
with
M_{1}\to N
, then:

\displaystyle\left\lfloor{\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x::y\allowbreak=\allowbreak M_{1}\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak M_{2}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M_{2}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(y_{1},[y_{2},\dots,y_{n}],|\Phi|){\scriptstyle{\text{ where }[y_{1},\dots,y_{n}]=\left\lfloor{M_{1}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)}}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{M_{2}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(y_{1},[y_{2},\dots,y_{n}],|\Phi|){\scriptstyle{\text{ where }[y_{1},\dots,y_{n}]=\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)}}

\displaystyle=\left\lfloor{\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x::y\allowbreak=\allowbreak N\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak M_{2}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

–

If
M\to N[x/M_{1}][y/M_{2}]
with
M^{\prime}=M_{1}::M_{2}
, then:

\displaystyle\left\lfloor{\mathtt{for\ }{k}\mathtt{\ in\ }{M_{1}\ ::\ M_{2}}\mathtt{\ do\ }{N}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{x,y,\Phi}(y_{1},[y_{2},\dots,y_{n}],|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{N}\right\rfloor_{x,y,\Phi}(M_{1},M_{2},|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\left\lfloor{N[M_{1}/x][M_{2}/y]}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)

\displaystyle=\left\lfloor{N[M_{1}/x][M_{2}/y]}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

where
[y_{1},\dots,y_{n}]=\left\lfloor{M_{1}::M_{2}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}(|\Phi|)
.

•

If
M=\mathtt{range\ }\ @n\ @M_{2}
then:

\displaystyle\left\lfloor{\mathtt{range\ }@n@m}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\bigtimes_{i=n}^{m-1}i

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\begin{cases}[]\text{ if }n-m=0\\
n\times\bigtimes_{i=n+1}^{m-1}i\text{ otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle=|\Phi|\mapsto\begin{cases}[]\text{ if }\left\lfloor{n-m}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}=0\\
\left\lfloor{n}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}\times\left\lfloor{\mathtt{range\ }@(n+1)@m)}\right\rfloor\text{ otherwise}\end{cases}

\displaystyle=\left\lfloor{\mathtt{ifz\ }{m-n}\mathtt{\ then\ }{\mathtt{VNil}}\mathtt{\ else\ }{n\ ::\mathtt{range\ }\ @(n+1)\ @m}}\right\rfloor_{\Phi}

\square

Lemma
.

​
(
4.3
)

The translation procedure is correct in respect to the operational semantics.
If
A
is a translatable type,
\Phi,\Gamma\vdash M:A
, and
M\to N
,
then
\left\llbracket{M}\right\rrbracket_{\Phi,\Gamma}=\left\llbracket{N}\right\rrbracket_{\Phi,\Gamma}
.

Proof
.

By case analysis on the reductions of translatable terms.

•

If
M=(\lambda x^{A}.M^{\prime})V
and
N=M^{\prime}[V/x]
,

\left\llbracket{(\lambda x^{A}.M^{\prime})V}\right\rrbracket_{\Phi,\Delta,\Gamma}=|\Phi|\mapsto\hbox to111.26pt{\vbox to52.38pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 57.40552pt\lower-21.53957pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \hbox to0.0pt{

•

If
M=\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x^{A}::y^{\mathtt{Vec}\ {n}\ {A}}\allowbreak=\allowbreak V_{1}::V_{2}\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak M^{\prime}
and

=\left\llbracket{\mathtt{ifz\ }{N^{\prime}}\mathtt{\ then\ }{M^{\prime}\ ;\ \star}\mathtt{\ else\ }{\mathtt{let\ }\allowbreak x::xs^{\prime}\allowbreak=\allowbreak M^{\prime}\mathtt{\ in\ }\allowbreak x\ ;\ \mathtt{drop}\ @(N^{\prime}-1)\ xs^{\prime}}}\right\rrbracket_{\Phi,\Gamma}

•

If
M\to N
is an internal reduction of a translatable term,
then the diagrams result equivalent via the inductive hypothesis.

•

If
M\to N
is an internal reduction of an evaluable term,
then the diagrams result equivalent via the inductive hypothesis
and Lemma
4.2
.

\square
